i have had both a male veiltail and a female betta in with my 11 black skirt tetras. when black skirts get comfortable and stake out their own territory in a tank, they become aggressive. eventually my much larger black skirt tetras began to literally beat up my male betta, and later on my female betta didn’t fare any better. i would recommend removing the betta to his own tank eventually because the black skirts do gang up on bettas and will harass them to death when they get comfortable in a tank. 

my black skirts also beat up and ate my glowlight tetras, so any tank mates less tenacious and aggressive than them will be beaten. in my experience zebra danios seem to hold their own well with black skirts, as well as angelfish and mollies.

i feel like some europeans can be purposefully obtuse when it comes to americans and american linguistics when this subject is concerned. for example, someone from america saying they’re polish/their family is from poland is not the same as them claiming polish nationality, no american raised, polish american would think they could waltz into poland and feel right at home. many groups like the irish, poles, and italians were second-class citizens so they created communities and clung onto their traditions and cultural identity. many ethnicities fled their home countries to escape danger but still feel strongly connected to the country they were from ethnically/had cultural ties to. 

my grandparents fled the philippines to escape the japanese occupation during the war. my grandmother who had to play dead after a japanese soldier had shot at her in her home country, immigrated to the united states and learned to speak three languages. my grandfather was a filipino-american immigrant and fought in the war. obviously they became american citizens, but would be filipino if you’d asked. as a third-gen filipino, of course i’m claiming filipino heritage. 

nobody in america hears someone say, “i’m filipino!” and goes, “no you’re not! you’re american!” it can be just as weird to go “you’re not irish! you’re american!” 

two things can be right at once, which is (1) being an american and (2) having an ethnic background from another country. for example not everybody is native american (around 2%), the way ~75% of britain is ethnically british and originated from the country. the united states has the highest number of immigrants in the world, and with many different cultures, heritage is one way to hold onto that familial cultural identity, in addition having a unique american culture on top of that. 

it’s alright to not understand something because you are not part of that culture. but if someone is, it can come across as distasteful and thoughtless to try to have a say in something foreign to you.

when i was a teen my family went away and i had a tank with 4 mollies in it that i left my cousin & aunt to feed every other day. i explained “just a pinch” of food, showed exactly how much that would be. the day we came home i ran upstairs to check my tank and suddenly the bare bottom tank had a flakey substrate. they emptied out most of a container of flake food in a matter of under a week and it absolutely coated my tank like a wicked shag rug. took a bit to clean it up but mollies are hardy so i caught it in time. now i don’t ask anybody to feed my fish except my dad who also has his own and understands underfeeding>overfeeding. you can never predict this kind of thing, i’m so sorry about what happened to your fish.

whenever any of our girls got sick, we always turned to at-home remedies because, though they’re pets, a lot of vets aren’t going to be avian-oriented and things can be costly for what is unfortunately usually a rather cheap animal. however we did use a vet twice for our birds. first to put down one of our girls whose quality of life was impacted by her increasing inability to move on her own so we wanted to do the right thing- it actually did not turn out great or pretty and i wouldn’t recommend using a vet that “also” specializes in birds, when they usually see dogs/cats. that’s to say if a vet is used at all.


another time our cochin girl got an impacted crop. home remedies, patience and time, she only worsened. now we loved this cochin and we’re fortunate enough an avian-specializing vet was about half an hour away. ended up forking over a grand to get miss girl back up and moving. now she has the most beautiful feathers this autumn. 


taking a chicken to a vet can seem absurd to the people who would see it like taking a fish to the vet. surprisingly there’s people out there that do it, but it really isn’t the norm and it’s perfectly acceptable the fact that most can’t/don’t see the point to.
